newsitem.title: USA: NYS McCall calls planned tax cuts a gamble.
newsitem.headline: NYS McCall calls planned tax cuts a gamble.

text.p: The New York State Comptroller on Wednesday warned that Albany's preliminary budget for fiscal 1998 might run aground because its tax cuts were too big and it relied too heavily on borrowing.
H. Carl McCall, in prepared remarks, pointed out that only $200 million of the $4.75 billion of proposed tax reductions would be accounted for in the present fiscal year, which started on April 1.
"That's a gamble -- a gamble New York has taken before and lost," McCall said.

Gov. George Pataki, a Republican, defended his budget as prudently balanced, saying it did not rely on unrealistic projections for Wall Street's powerhouses, which contribute a large share of the state's revenues.

New York State's top elected fiscal monitor, a potential Democrat challenger in next year's gubernatorial race, also pounced on the new pact for not dealing with the long-term gap between how much the state collects and how much it spends.

"No steps are being taken to address the state's structural deficit. The state still is doing too much back-door borrowing for things that should be paid for on a pay-as-you go basis. Nothing is being done to improve New York's rock-bottom credit rating," McCall said.

Bob Kurtter, a credit analyst with Moody's Investors Service, made some of the same criticisms. "Our concern is the combination of increased spending for ongoing programs coupled with (continuing) tax cuts will exacerbate out-year budget gaps in years that Wall Street is not booming and the economy is not as robust."

Kurtter added that it was too early to say how the rating agency would respond to the new pact, noting it had yet to be enacted by the legislature, and that he had not yet had time to conduct an in-depth analysis of it. He said, "The strength of the revenue picture at this point in the game certainly indicates the state will have positive revenues and fiscal results in the near-term."

The state comptroller also homed in on Albany's failure to approve a budget on time for the 13th year in a row, with a sarcastic recommendation that lawmakers should take a one- to two-day holiday after they complete the present budget, and then start thrashing out next year's agreement. Legislators were expected to begin enacting the new pact on Friday, a job that might take most of the weekend.
